steps.label: Faster backprop
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp08 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 10 pages; this unit is self-study and is not taught in class; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Narrow valley
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP08, a self-study unit. Prerequisites: gradient descent (KP06, KP07), where each step goes against the gradient by the learning rate mu times the gradient; contour lines, which join points of equal cost and are denser where the cost changes faster; and the bowl shape of a quadratic. Curvature is how sharply the cost surface bends; a narrow valley (an ill-conditioned surface) has a very large curvature in one direction and a very small one in the other, so the contours are flat ellipses. The example is designed for this lecture: J equals one half of w1 squared plus 20 w2 squared, curvature 20 along w2 and 1 along w1, start (-4, 1), mu equal to 0.08. Plain gradient descent needs 100 steps to reach |w| below 0.001, and the path swings up and down along w2 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers why the path zigzags.

steps.label: Why it zigzags
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the narrow valley. This page separates the two directions. In the steep direction the gradient of w2 is 20 w2, so the update w2 minus 0.08 times 20 times w2 equals minus 0.6 w2: the sign flips every step and the value shrinks only to 0.6 times, 1, minus 0.6, 0.36, minus 0.216. In the flat direction w1 becomes 0.92 w1, the same direction and only 8% smaller per step. The dilemma is that mu must stay below 2 over 20, which is 0.1, so that w2 does not swing wider; with mu equal to 0.12 the factor is 1 minus 2.4, equal to minus 1.4, and after 60 steps |w| has reached 5.86 times 10 to the 8 (computed by program). But so small a step makes w1 crawl. Next, the next page covers the momentum term.

steps.label: Momentum term
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on why the path zigzags. This page defines momentum. Momentum lets the update carry inertia: besides this gradient step it adds alpha times the previous update, so delta w at t equals alpha times delta w at t minus 1 minus mu times g at t; alpha is the momentum factor, 0.1 to 0.8 in practice, and alpha equal to 0 is plain gradient descent. By hand with mu equal to 0.08, alpha equal to 0.6 and start (-4, 1): step 1 gives the update (0.32, minus 1.6) and w equal to (minus 3.68, minus 0.6); step 2 is 0.6 times (0.32, minus 1.6) minus 0.08 times (minus 3.68, minus 12), equal to (0.4864, 0), where the w2 inertia of minus 0.96 and the gradient part of 0.96 cancel exactly; step 3 gives (0.5473, 0.96) and w equal to (minus 2.646, 0.36). Next, the next page covers why momentum works.

steps.label: Why it works
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the momentum term. This page expands the momentum formula. An exponentially weighted average gives the latest gradient the largest weight and multiplies older ones by alpha at every step back, so the weights are 1, alpha, alpha squared, and so on. Expanding T steps, delta w at T equals minus mu times the sum of alpha to the t times g at T minus t, plus alpha to the T times delta w at 0, and the last term vanishes within a few steps. With a constant gradient (the flat direction) the total weight 1 plus alpha plus alpha squared and so on equals 1 over 1 minus alpha: 2.5 times for alpha 0.6 and 5 times for alpha 0.8 (verified by 80 steps with a fixed gradient, computed by program). With alternating gradients (the steep direction) the weights alternate in sign and the average cancels. Next, the next page covers the comparison of two paths.

steps.label: Two paths
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on why momentum works. This page compares the two paths. With the same start (-4, 1) and mu equal to 0.08, plain gradient descent needs 100 steps to reach |w| below 0.001 and momentum with alpha 0.6 needs 28 (computed by program); 28 over 100 is 0.28, about 3.6 times faster. The red path swings many times along w2 while the green swing shrinks faster and w1 also advances faster. The price is one more stored vector, the previous update, and one more knob, alpha. Next, the next page covers the best value of α.

steps.label: Best α
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the comparison of two paths. This page dispels the myth that a larger alpha is always better. Steps needed at mu equal to 0.08 (computed by program): alpha 0 gives 100, 0.3 gives 65, 0.5 gives 36, 0.6 gives 28, 0.7 gives 44, 0.8 gives 63, 0.9 gives 137 and 0.95 gives 247. Alpha of 0.9 or more is slower than no momentum: the inertia is so large that it overshoots the valley floor and swings like a pendulum for a long time. In practice 0.1 to 0.8 is common; the best value depends on the problem and must be tried, and the source reports speed-ups of 2 times or more. Next, the next page covers the adaptive learning rate.

steps.label: Adaptive rate
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the best value of α. This page lets the learning rate adjust itself. The adaptive learning rate looks at the ratio of successive costs J: when the ratio is below 1 (better) mu is multiplied by 1.05; when it is above 1.04 (worse) mu is multiplied by 0.7, the step is rejected and the momentum is reset; otherwise nothing changes. It is asymmetric: grow slowly when things improve, brake hard when they worsen. Results (computed by program): with initial mu0 of 0.02 plain descent needs 411 steps and the adaptive rule 61; with mu0 of 0.12 plain descent blows up while the adaptive rule converges in 95 steps in all, 12 of them rejected; mu0 of 0.08 is already near the best, 100 steps against 93, hardly better. Next, the next page covers quickprop.

steps.label: quickprop
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the adaptive learning rate. This page introduces quickprop: treat every weight as independent, estimate the parabola's floor from the last two slopes and jump straight there. The formula: delta w at t equals alpha at t times delta w at t minus 1, where alpha at t is the smaller of g at t over g at t minus 1 minus g at t, and the cap 1.75. In the example for w2, step 1 is a plain step from 1 to minus 0.6 and the slope goes from 20 to minus 12; alpha equals minus 12 over 20 plus 12, which is minus 0.375, and delta equals minus 0.375 times minus 1.6, which is plus 0.6, so step 2 lands exactly on 0 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the five methods and Newton's method.

steps.label: Five methods
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on quickprop. This page compares the steps of five methods (computed by program): plain at mu 0.02 needs 411, adaptive 61, plain at mu 0.08 needs 100, momentum 28 and quickprop 5. But here every slice is exactly a parabola, which suits quickprop best; real costs are not quadratic, and every speed-up costs complexity. Extension: Newton's method uses curvature (the Hessian matrix H of second derivatives) to compute the floor directly, delta w equals minus H inverse times g, and a quadratic needs one step; here H equals diag(1, 20), delta w equals minus w and one step reaches the origin, at the price of computing, storing and inverting the Hessian. quickprop can be seen as a one-dimensional Newton step per weight. Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the five methods and Newton's method. Two exercises on the same valley with mu 0.08 and alpha 0.6; after step 2, w equals (minus 3.1936, minus 0.6) and the step-2 update is (0.4864, 0). Q1: the gradient g equals (w1, 20 w2), which is (minus 3.1936, 20 times minus 0.6), equal to (minus 3.1936, minus 12). Q2: delta w at 3 equals 0.6 times (0.4864, 0) minus 0.08 times (minus 3.1936, minus 12), equal to (0.29184 plus 0.25549, 0.96), which is (0.5473, 0.96); w equals (minus 3.1936 plus 0.5473, minus 0.6 plus 0.96), equal to (minus 2.6463, 0.36). Check: w2 did not move in step 2, so its inertia is 0 and the whole 0.96 from the gradient becomes displacement (computed by program). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
